product.title: Bulgarian 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Bulgarian: a stressed, English-friendly pronunciation guide printed right above every Cyrillic word, short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Bulgarian builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Includes a table of the Bulgarian Cyrillic alphabet, an explanation of the letter ъ, a summary of the definite article that sticks to the end of the word, A1 verb tables, and a glossary. Written with English speakers in mind — each unit targets one typical stumbling block, from the verb "to be" that may never start a sentence to the possessive that follows the noun.

blocks.text: Bulgarian is the easiest Slavic language to learn, and almost nobody knows it. The Slavic family's reputation was built by Russian and Polish: six or seven cases, nouns that change shape depending on their role in the sentence, rows and rows of endings to memorize. People see Cyrillic on the shop signs in Sofia, remember that story, and decide the language is out of reach.

In fact Bulgarian **threw that whole case system away** — the only Slavic language to do so (together with its close neighbor Macedonian). Bulgarian nouns don't change form. *Град* (city) stays *град* whether it's the subject, the object, or follows a preposition. What needs six different forms in Russian needs just one form plus a preposition in Bulgarian — exactly the way English works.

The alphabet, too, is the easiest part of the whole journey, not the hardest. Thirty letters, one letter one sound, with almost no exceptions. Most people who are serious can read Cyrillic haltingly in one afternoon and fluently within a week. Compare English, where *though*, *through*, *tough* and *thought* use the same string of letters for four different sounds. And one point of pride deserves a mention on page one: **the Cyrillic alphabet was born in Bulgaria**, at the Preslav literary school at the end of the ninth century. Russian, Ukrainian, Serbian and Mongolian all borrowed it from here.

In return, Bulgarian asks for two things its neighbors don't have. The first is a **definite article stuck to the end of the word**: *книга* means "book", *книгата* means "the book" — English "the", moved to the back and glued on. The second is the **missing infinitive**. There's no equivalent of "to eat" as a base form standing on its own; instead there's *да ям* — "that I eat". Both will feel strange for three units, and then stop feeling strange at all.

This course was written with English speakers' habits in mind. You get one thing for free: like English and unlike Russian, Bulgarian **must use "to be"** — *Аз съм студент*, "I am a student". The traps lie elsewhere: that verb has strict rules about where it may stand, the article goes on the end, and the noun's gender matters from the very first unit. Each unit in this course targets one point like that.

Bulgarian is spoken by about seven million people in Bulgaria and several million more abroad, and it's one of the official languages of the European Union. Once you have it, Macedonian practically opens up by itself, and much of Serbian and Croatian becomes guessable. More importantly: this country almost never meets foreigners who speak its language. Your first sentence will be remembered all day.
Twenty units. One unit per sitting. Start today, not tomorrow — and don't start with the alphabet table, start with Unit 1. The letters will stick as you go.

This course has twenty units. Each unit is designed for one sitting — about twenty to thirty minutes — and contains one dialogue, notes on that dialogue, one to three grammar boxes, vocabulary, four exercises and their answers. If you do one unit a day, you'll finish in three weeks. Three units a week, in seven weeks. Both are fine; what isn't fine is doing five units in one day and then stopping for a month.
How to work through a unit

items: **Read the dialogue once, only the Cyrillic line and its pronunciation.** Don't look at the translation. You won't understand it, and that's part of the design — your ears need to meet the sounds before your brain meets the meaning.
**Read it again, looking at the free translation on the right.** Now the content sinks in.

**Read it a third time along with the literal line.** This line is the most valuable thing in the whole course: it shows Bulgarian structure as it really is, including the parts a neat translation hides.
**Read the notes and the grammar boxes.** The notes explain things you've just seen, not things you haven't met yet.
**Read the dialogue out loud one more time.** Out loud, not in your head. Bulgarian has sounds English doesn't, and your mouth needs practice your eyes can't give it.
**Do the four exercises on paper.** On paper, not in your head. Writing Cyrillic by hand is the fastest way to make the letters stick.
**Only then check the answer key.** Note down your mistakes, don't just correct them.

blocks.text: Four things that make people fail at this language

items: **Putting off the alphabet.** Reading only through the pronunciation line feels comfortable for a week, then becomes a prison. Cover the pronunciation line from Unit 5 on.
**Memorizing word lists without sentences.** Words learned alone evaporate. Words used in sentences stay.
**Looking for one-to-one equivalents in English.** Some things simply have none — the *да* form is one of them. Accept first, understand later.
**Keeping quiet for fear of mistakes.** Bulgarians almost never meet foreigners who try their language. Your mistakes won't be laughed at; your effort will be appreciated out of all proportion.

blocks.title: What you can do after Unit 20
items: Read and write Cyrillic without spelling it out; about three hundred and fifty active words; the definite article in three genders and the plural; present, past and future tenses; the *да* form in place of the infinitive; short and long possessives; and the ability to handle everyday business — introducing yourself, ordering food, bargaining at the market, asking the way, going to the doctor, and telling what you did yesterday.

front.title: Bulgarian Cyrillic: thirty letters in three piles

blocks.text: The fastest way to master Cyrillic isn't memorizing the alphabet in order, but sorting it into three piles: letters you already know, letters that **pretend** you know them, and letters that are genuinely new. The first pile is free, the third needs practice, and the second is where all the mistakes happen.
Pile 1 — same shape, same sound (free)
Pile 2 — deceptive shapes (⚠️ where all the mistakes happen)
These six letters look like Latin letters you know and sound completely different. If you learn only these six rows today, ninety percent of your reading mistakes are already gone.
Pile 3 — new shapes, familiar sounds

blocks.title: ⚠️ Bulgarian Щ is not like Russian Щ
items: If you've learned some Russian, the letter **щ** there is a long, soft *sh*. In Bulgarian it is always **two sounds: sh + t**, as in *fresh tea*. *Още* is pronounced *OSH-teh*, not *osh-eh*. *Пощата* (the post office) is pronounced *POSH-ta-ta*. It's the quickest way to tell someone who has really learned Bulgarian from someone guessing from Russian.

blocks.text: Two letters that aren't ordinary sounds

head: Letter
Its job
rows: This is a **full vowel**, not a silent sign as in Russian — the sound of *u* in *but* or *a* in *sofa*. The next page is all about this letter.

Appears only in the combination **ьо**, and only after a consonant: *шофьор* (sho-FYOR) — driver. Its only job is to soften the consonant before it. You'll meet it maybe ten times in the whole course.

blocks.text: Thirty letters, in alphabetical order. The "Say it" column uses the spelling used consistently throughout this course. In it, **и** is written *ee*, **у** is *oo*, an **е** at the end of a syllable is *eh* (not "ee"), and **ай** is *ai*. Cover the column with paper and test yourself until nothing trips you up.
The six most common reading mistakes

blocks.title: Handwriting
items: Cyrillic handwriting differs quite a lot from print, and Bulgarian has some handwritten forms that differ from Russian. At A1 you don't need to master it — just write in print letters, as Bulgarians themselves do when they want to be read clearly. What matters is **a moving hand**, not the style.

front.title: Ъ and stress: two things that change everything

blocks.text: If you read only one page of this introduction, read this one. These two things decide whether Bulgarians recognize your sentences or not, and neither is written on any page of any book in Bulgaria — so there's nowhere else to learn them.
1. Ъ — the vowel of "but"

The letter **ъ** is a vowel sound with no symbol in the Latin alphabet. The good news: English is full of it. **ъ is the *u* in *but* and *cup*, or the *a* in *sofa* and *about*** — the relaxed "uh" sound. You make it hundreds of times a day; the only new thing is the symbol.
Throughout this course **ъ is written ă** in the pronunciation line. When you see *ă*, say the "uh" of *but* and you're right.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Ъ also hides in endings
items: The masculine definite article is written **-ът** and pronounced *-ăt*: *градът* = *gra-DĂT* (the city). The short form is written **-а** but still pronounced *-ă*: *града* = *gra-DĂ*. So the letter **а** at the end of a definite masculine noun **is not pronounced *a***. This is the only place where Bulgarian spelling truly lies, and this course always prints the correct pronunciation above it.

blocks.text: 2. Stress — unwritten, and it can change meaning

English speakers know that stress matters: *REcord* and *reCORD* are different words. Bulgarian takes this further: stress can fall on any syllable, it's never marked in everyday writing, and in a number of words it's **the only thing that tells two meanings apart**.

That's why **every Bulgarian word in this course comes with a pronunciation in which the stressed syllable is in capitals**: *[къща|KĂSH-ta]*. Learn each word together with its stress from the start — fixing a stress you've learned wrong is much harder than learning it right once.
Unstressed vowels shift
Unstressed vowels weaken, as in Russian but much more lightly. Three tendencies you should know — not to memorize, just so you aren't surprised when you hear them:

items: **unstressed а leans toward ъ**: *жена* sounds like *zheh-NĂ*, not a crisp *zheh-NA*.
**unstressed о leans toward у**: *молив* (pencil) sounds halfway to *MOO-leev*.
**unstressed е leans toward и**: *петел* (rooster) sounds like *pee-TEL*.

blocks.text: This course does **not** write that weakening in the pronunciation line — if it did, you couldn't trace the spelling back to the original letters. What's written is the full sound plus the stress. If you pronounce full vowels in every syllable, you'll sound a little too clear, and that's no problem at all — Bulgarian newsreaders do the same.

back.title: The definite article on one page

blocks.text: This page is for *checking*, not for *learning*. Once you've finished the twenty units, you'll have used everything here in sentences; this table just tidies it up.
Long form vs short form (masculine singular only)

head: Form
Used when the word…
Example
rows: Град**ът** е голям. — The city is big.
everything else: object, after a preposition
Виждам град**а**. / в град**а** — I see the city. / in the city.

blocks.text: ⚠️ This rule **applies only to masculine singular**. Feminine, neuter and plural have just one form. And in everyday speech Bulgarians themselves often use the short form everywhere — the long/short rule is a rule of writing. Don't let it stop your mouth.
Adjectives take the article too — and only the first word gets it
⚠️ The article moves to the adjective and the noun goes bare: **големият град**, not *големият градът*. A phrase can carry only one article, and it always sticks to the **first** word.

blocks.title: When to use the article — three practical rules
items: **Use it** when the thing has already been mentioned, or it's clear to both sides which one, or there's only one in the world (слънцето — the sun).
**Use it too** for nouns meant generally, as a category: *Кафето е скъпо* — coffee (in general) is expensive. English uses no article here; Bulgarian does.

**Don't use it** after *един/една/едно* (one, a), with a noun that's just being introduced, and don't add a second one after a short possessive — *книгата ми* is already definite through *-та*, nothing else needed.

blocks.text: Present tense — three groups

The group is decided by **the vowel before the third-person singular ending**: -е → Group I, -и → Group II, -а → Group III. Group III is the biggest and the most regular; if you meet a new verb ending in **-ам** or **-ям**, it's almost certainly Group III.
Съм — the verb "to be"
⚠️ The present forms **can never stand at the start of a sentence**. *Съм студент* is wrong; the right forms are *Аз съм студент* or *Студент съм*.
Past tense (аорист) — completed events
Future tense — ще + present form
One little word, **ще**, goes in front of the present form, and that's it. *Ще работя* — I will work. The negative isn't *не ще* but **няма да**: *Няма да работя* — I won't work.
The perfect — съм + participle

head: Person
Form
Meaning
rows: I have been / I have worked
we have been / we have worked

blocks.text: ⚠️ The participle **agrees with the speaker's gender**, just like the Russian past tense. A woman says *работила съм*, a man *работил съм*.
Numbers 0–20
The full forms *единадесет, дванадесет, двадесет* are used in formal writing; in conversation everyone uses the short forms *единайсет, дванайсет, двайсет*. Use the short ones.
Tens, hundreds, thousands

blocks.title: ⚠️ Two kinds of forms for 1 and 2
items: **Един/една/едно** follows the noun's gender: *един стол* (one chair, m), *една книга* (one book, f), *едно дете* (one child, n).
**Два** for masculine, **две** for feminine and neuter: *два стола*, *две книги*, *две деца*.
For **men** there's a special form: *двама мъже* (two men), *трима братя* (three brothers). It's only for male people, never for things.

blocks.text: Telling the time

⚠️ *Три и половина* literally means "three and a half" and means **3:30** — like English "half past three". If you know German, beware: *halb vier* is also 3:30 but names the next hour. Bulgarian always counts forward from the hour it names.
Days and months

Monday to Friday literally mean "the day after the rest day" (*по-неделник*), "second" (*вторник*), "middle" (*сряда*), "fourth" (*четвъртък*), "fifth" (*петък*) — a numbered system like Portuguese *segunda-feira*. *Неделя* itself literally means "no-work".
Personal pronouns in three forms
The short forms are the everyday ones; the long forms are only for emphasis or after a preposition. *Виждам го* (I see him) — normal. *Виждам него, не нея* (I see **him**, not her) — emphatic.
Possessives — short and long

blocks.title: The short form is your best friend
items: *Книгата ми* works like "the book of mine": the noun first, the possessive stuck on behind. The one thing to remember — the noun must first take the article (*книга* → *книгата*), then *ми* follows.
For the closest family members, the article is **not** used: *майка ми* (my mother), *баща ми* (my father), *брат ми* (my brother) — not *майката ми*.

blocks.text: Question words

⚠️ Bulgarian doesn't use different question words for **"where"** and **"where to"** — both are *къде*, just like English "where", and the verb makes it clear. Good news: Russian does distinguish them (*где* vs *куда*), and beginners always mix them up.
The words you'll need most at A1, in English alphabetical order. Stress is marked by capitals in the pronunciation, and **ă** is always the "uh" of *but*.

If you've reached this page after working through twenty units, you have something real: Cyrillic you can read without spelling it out, about three hundred and fifty active words, the definite article in all its forms, present, past and future tenses, the *да* form in place of the infinitive, and the ability to handle everyday business without switching to English. That's a complete A1, not half an A1.
Three things waiting for you at A2

items: **Аорист vs имперфект.** Bulgarian has two simple past tenses, and this course deliberately teaches only one. The second — the *имперфект* — is for ongoing situations in the past: *четях* (I was reading) vs *четох* (I read it to the end).

**Преизказно наклонение — the hearsay mood.** This is Bulgarian's most famous feature, one almost no other European language has: a verb form that marks that you **didn't witness** the event yourself. *Той дойде* = he came (I saw it). *Той дошъл* = he came, apparently. News, gossip and fairy tales all use it. Unit 20 gives you a peek; A2 teaches it properly.
**Verb aspect as a full system.** Every verb has a completed and an uncompleted partner — *пиша / напиша*. At A1 you use them piece by piece; at A2 they become a system.

blocks.text: What you can do this very week

items: **Switch your phone to Bulgarian for three days.** You already know where all the buttons are, so there's no risk of getting lost — and thirty interface words stick effortlessly.
**Listen to БНР Хоризонт or a Bulgarian podcast for ten minutes a day** without trying to understand. What you're training is an ear that recognizes where words begin and end, not comprehension.
**Write five sentences a day about your day** using the past tense from Unit 15. Five sentences, not fifty.
**Find one person to talk to.** Bulgaria has lively online communities that rarely meet foreign learners. You'll be treated like a guest of honor.

blocks.title: One sentence to take home
items: *Не се притеснявай — говори!* (neh seh pree-tes-nya-VAI — go-VO-ree) — "Don't be shy — speak!" It's the sentence you'll hear most from Bulgarians once they know you're learning their language. Trust them.

blocks.text: If you'd like to continue with a teacher, Linguo offers private Bulgarian classes from A2 up. But don't wait for a class to start speaking. This course is already enough for your first day in Sofia.
